core: working definition of organizational structure, attributed: organizing coordinates and allocates a firm's resources so it can carry out its plans and achieve its goals, and the result is a formal structure — the order and design of relationships within a company, with well-defined lines of authority, channels for information flow, and means of control (OpenStax Introduction to Business 7.1)

the Investopedia framing: an organizational structure is a system that guides how certain activities are directed to achieve the goals of an organization and determines how information flows between levels within the company

the organization chart: a visual representation of the structured relationships among tasks and the people given the authority to do those tasks; the chain of command can be traced on it from the CEO down to employees producing goods and services
four common structures named, each with one line and when it fits: functional, divisional, matrix, flat
authority in simple terms: the chain of command, the unity-of-command principle, and span of control — the number of employees one manager directly supervises
centralization versus decentralization: decisions concentrated at the top versus decision-making authority pushed down the hierarchy, with trade-offs
why structure matters: it shapes speed, communication, and accountability, with an original example (Harbor Hardware versus Branchline Hardware)
the honest framing: structures are tools, not cages — they change as the business grows
supporting: the organizing process builds structure in three steps: division of labor, departmentalization, and delegation (OpenStax 7.1)
traditional structures group employees by function, product, process, customer, or region and are more rigid; contemporary and team-based structures are more flexible
matrix structure trade-offs: dual chain of command, teamwork, efficient use of specialists, flexibility (OpenStax 7.2)
factors that set the optimal span of control: task complexity, worker location, delegation ability, interaction and feedback needed, worker skill and motivation (OpenStax 7.5)
accountability moves upward as managers at each level answer for the actions of their subordinates (OpenStax 7.4)
flat structures give employees autonomy and high speed of implementation and are common among startups (Investopedia)

claims.claim: Organizing involves coordinating and allocating a firm's resources so the firm can carry out its plans and achieve its goals; the result is a formal structure within the organization — the order and design of relationships within a company, with well-defined lines of authority, channels for information flow, and means of control.

An organizational structure is a system that guides how certain activities are directed to achieve the goals of an organization, and it determines how information flows between levels within the company (Investopedia).

An organization chart is a visual representation of the structured relationships among tasks and the people given the authority to do those tasks; the chain of command is shown in the organization chart and can be traced from the CEO all the way down to the employees producing goods and services.

Common structures include functional (grouping by primary function such as marketing, production, finance), divisional (grouping by product, customer, or region — OpenStax's product departmentalization, as in ITT's four product divisions), matrix (combining functional and product grouping so each employee has two supervisors, a functional line manager and a project manager), and flat (few or no middle layers, more employee autonomy, high speed of implementation).

The chain of command is the line of authority that extends from one level of the organization to the next, from top to bottom, and makes clear who reports to whom; under the unity of command principle everyone reports to and gets instructions from only one boss.

A manager's span of control is the number of employees the manager directly supervises; it can be as narrow as two or three employees or as wide as fifty or more, and the optimal span depends on task complexity, worker locations, the manager's ability to delegate, the interaction and feedback required, and the skill and motivation of the workers.

Centralization is the degree to which formal authority is concentrated in one area or level of the organization, where top management makes most key decisions (benefits: broad view, tight financial controls, lower cost from less redundancy; costs: stunted lower-level decision skills, slower response to customers). Decentralization pushes decision-making authority down the hierarchy, giving lower-level personnel more responsibility and power (benefits: quicker decisions, innovation, flexibility, faster manager development, job satisfaction; risks: costly mistakes, inefficient communication, competing objectives).

Accountability moves upward in the organization as managers in each successively higher level are held accountable for the actions of their subordinates; structure therefore determines where accountability sits.

Every organization has some kind of underlying structure; some connections are long-lasting while others can be changed at almost any time, and managers must first consider what kind of work needs to be done within the firm before choosing a structural framework — structures change as the business grows.

conflictingEvidence: No conflicts found between OpenStax and Investopedia on the core claims. Investopedia additionally lists team-based and network structures among common types and describes circular structures; those types are out of scope for this literacy-level lesson, which names the four most common (functional, divisional, matrix, flat) as required by the topic brief.
